lessons.title: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not

blocks.md:
Recall from the previous course: a softmax attention layer keeps every past token's key and value in a **KV cache**, so it can look any of them up exactly, but the cache grows with every token. A linear attention or state space model (**SSM**) layer instead folds each token into a **fixed-size state** (a matrix memory), so memory and per-token compute stay constant no matter how long the context gets.

A **hybrid model** stacks both kinds of layers in one network. To see why anyone would bother, we first need to see what the fixed state gives up.

blocks.title: Growing KV cache vs fixed state (toy, 8 tokens)

scenes.caption: After 2 tokens the attention layer has stored 2 separate entries. The SSM layer has 4 state slots, and both tokens are already blended into all of them.
After 4 tokens: 4 cache entries, still 4 state slots. Each slot is now a mixture of tokens 1 to 4.
After 8 tokens the cache has doubled again while the state has not grown. Simplified: real states hold from about 0.1 to 1 million numbers per layer, but they still have a fixed size.

blocks.md: A fixed state behaves like an associative memory with limited capacity. Take the simplest version from linear attention: write each pair with $S \mathrel{+}= v k^\top$ and read with $S k$. With $d$-dimensional random unit keys, every other stored pair adds **crosstalk** to the read: a bit of its value leaks into the answer. We measure the damage with cosine similarity, the dot product of two vectors divided by their lengths, which is 1 when the read points exactly along the stored value and near 0 when it is mostly noise.

Here is where the formula below comes from. Store $n$ pairs and read with key $k_j$: $S k_j = v_j (k_j^\top k_j) + \sum_{i \ne j} v_i (k_i^\top k_j)$. In words, the read is $v_j$ times the dot product of $k_j$ with itself, plus, for every other pair $i$, $v_i$ times the dot product of $k_i$ with $k_j$. The first term is exactly $v_j$, because $k_j$ has length 1. Each other term is $v_i$ scaled by the dot product of two random unit keys, which averages 0 and whose square averages $1/d$ (turn the axes so one key lies on the first axis: the dot product is then the other key's first coordinate, and the squares of its $d$ coordinates sum to 1, so each averages $1/d$). The $n - 1$ leaks point in random directions, so their squared lengths add: the noise has squared length about $(n-1)/d$ and is nearly orthogonal to $v_j$. The read is $v_j$ plus that noise, so its dot product with $v_j$ is 1 and its length is $\sqrt{1 + (n-1)/d}$, giving the cosine below. For $d = 8$ and $n = 8$ that is 1 over the square root of 1.875, about 0.73.

blocks.caption: In words: the cosine between the read and the stored value is about 1 over the square root of 1 plus (n minus 1) over d. It agrees with a simulation averaged over thousands of trials (d = 8 and 32, n from 1 to 128) to within about 0.02.

blocks.title: Recall quality of a d x d state as pairs pile up

scenes.caption: With d = 8, storing 8 pairs already drops recall similarity to about 0.75, and 64 pairs to 0.33. The cache keeps every pair, so a sharp attention can retrieve it exactly.
Quadrupling the state to d = 32 pushes the curve right (0.58 at 64 pairs) but the shape is the same: any fixed state eventually blurs. Drag d to see it.
Simplified: Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet add decay and smarter writes, which help choose what to keep, but they cannot store an unbounded number of exact pairs in a bounded state.

blocks.prompt: NVIDIA trained 8B-parameter Transformer, Mamba and Mamba-2 models on the same 1.1T tokens and gave them a phone book, then asked for one person's number. The Transformer is near 100% up to its 4096-token training length. Where do the pure SSMs start failing?
blocks.reveal: Far earlier: both start answering incorrectly beyond roughly **500 tokens** of phone book (Waleffe et al., 2024). Their wrong answers share many digits with the right one, which the authors call **fuzzy memory**: the entry was compressed into the state, just not exactly. Training Mamba-2 on 3.5T tokens did not fix it.

blocks.md: AI21's Jamba paper saw the same weakness from another angle. At 1.3B parameters and 250B tokens, a pure Mamba model matched pure attention on perplexity but collapsed on few-shot tasks where the answer must follow the format of the examples. Perplexity is e raised to the model's average loss per token (the negative log of the probability it gave each true next token), so it reads as how many equally likely choices the model is torn between: lower is better. A few-shot task puts a handful of solved examples in the prompt before the real question, so the model must learn the task, including the exact answer words, from the prompt alone; this is called in-context learning, since no weights change. IMDB is a set of movie reviews labeled positive or negative (Maas et al., 2011). On IMDB the pure Mamba model often answered "Very Good" or "3/10" instead of the required "Positive" or "Negative".

Adding attention as 1 of every 8 layers fixed it, and the authors found attention heads in the hybrid that point from the final ":" token back to the label tokens of the few-shot examples, like induction heads. An induction head (Olsson et al., 2022) is an attention head that finds an earlier place where the current token appeared and copies the token that came next: having seen "A B" once, on seeing "A" again it predicts "B". That needs an exact lookup into the past, which a blurred fixed state cannot do.

blocks.title: Jamba ablation: pure Mamba fails where copying matters

scenes.caption: IMDB (few-shot sentiment), higher is better. Pure Mamba scores 48.8 because it ignores the answer format. The hybrid scores 90.9, above pure attention.
QuAC (question answering in context: a dialog where a student asks about a hidden Wikipedia section): the hybrid recovers most of the gap (26.6 vs 27.9 for attention, 20.2 for Mamba).
NarrativeQA (questions about stories from books and movie scripts): 45.8, 27.7 and 43.7. One attention layer in eight gets close to pure attention. All models: 1.3B parameters, 250B tokens.

blocks.md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

blocks.question: A pure SSM answers a phone-book query with 555-284-7710 when the true number is 555-284-7719. What does this suggest?
options: The entry was compressed into the fixed state but cannot be read back exactly
The model never saw the entry, so it guessed a random number
The tokenizer split the digits incorrectly
The model needs positional embeddings to count digits
blocks.explain: Waleffe et al. found SSM answers share many digits with the correct number: information about each entry is in the state, but crosstalk from everything else blurs it. That is the capacity limit of a fixed-size memory, not missing information.

blocks.question: Which task is least likely to separate a pure SSM from a Transformer of the same size and data?
options: Recalling a phone number listed 3,000 tokens earlier
Copying a long string from the prompt
Zero-shot commonsense multiple choice such as PIQA or HellaSwag
Few-shot classification that must reuse exact label strings
blocks.explain: PIQA asks which of two solutions achieves an everyday physical goal; HellaSwag asks for the most plausible ending of a described situation. On such zero-shot commonsense tasks Mamba and Mamba-2 matched or beat the Transformer in the NVIDIA 8B study. The other three all need exact retrieval or copying from the context, which is where fixed-state models fall behind.

lessons.title: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention

blocks.md:
Most recent hybrids (Mamba-2-Hybrid, Nemotron-H) use **Mamba-2** for their SSM layers; Jamba uses the original Mamba. Mamba-2 is easiest to understand as a close cousin of the gated linear attention you already know.

Per head, Mamba-2 keeps a state $h$ of shape (head dim $P$) x (state size $N$). Each token produces an input $x_t$ (like a value), a vector $B_t$ (like a key), a vector $C_t$ (like a query) and a step size $\Delta_t > 0$. The decay $A$ is a single learned negative number per head, so the whole state shrinks by one scalar per step.

blocks.tex: a_t = e^{\Delta_t A}, \qquad h_t = a_t\, h_{t-1} + \Delta_t\, x_t B_t^\top, \qquad y_t = h_t C_t + D\, x_t
blocks.caption: The decode step in the reference implementation (mamba_ssm, Mamba2.step). Compare gated linear attention: S_t = a_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^T and o_t = S_t q_t.

blocks.md: In words: each step multiplies the old state by $a_t = e^{\Delta_t A}$ (where that comes from is below), adds the input $x_t$ times the key-like $B_t$, scaled by the step size, and reads the output as the state times $C_t$, plus $D x_t$, a learned per-head skip that passes the input straight through. In code the step size is called dt. The names come from control theory: an SSM is a continuous-time system $dh/dt = A h + B x$. If a token's input is held for a time $\Delta_t$, the state decays by $e^{\Delta_t A}$ over that interval, and the input adds about $\Delta_t B x$. So $\Delta_t$ is how long the model lets each token last, and a negative $A$ keeps $a_t$ between 0 and 1.

The step size is input-dependent, which is what makes the layer **selective**: a large $\Delta_t$ makes $a_t$ close to 0 (forget the past, write the new token strongly), a small $\Delta_t$ keeps $a_t$ near 1 (hold memory). Step through a toy head with $P = 1$, $N = 2$ and $A = -1$.

blocks.title: One Mamba-2 head, 4 tokens, N = 2
blocks.code:
h = [0.0, 0.0]                       # state: N = 2 numbers
for x, dt, B, C in tokens:
    a = exp(-dt)                     # A = -1, so 0 < a < 1
    h = [a*hi + dt*x*bi for hi, bi in zip(h, B)]
    y = sum(ci*hi for ci, hi in zip(C, h))
    print(round(y, 3))

scenes.caption: Token 1: x = 1, dt = 0.5, B = [1, 0]. The write goes to slot 0: h = [0.5, 0]. C = [1, 0] reads slot 0, so y = 0.5.
Token 2: x = 2, dt = 0.5, B = [0, 1]. Slot 0 decays to 0.303 while slot 1 receives 1.0. C = [0, 1] reads it back: y = 1.0.
Token 3: x = 0, dt = 0.1, so a = 0.905: the head mostly holds memory. C = [1, 0] reads slot 0 and gets 0.274, a faded copy of token 1.
Token 4: x = 0 and dt = 3.0 give a = 0.05, which wipes the state. C = [0, 1] reads slot 1 and gets 0.045 instead of about 0.9. One scalar decides how much of everything is kept.

blocks.md: The Mamba-2 paper (Dao and Gu, 2024) shows the same layer can be computed in a second, attention-like way. Unroll the recurrence and the output is a masked attention with no softmax, where queries are $C$, keys are $B$ and the mask multiplies the decays between two positions. This is the **state space duality (SSD)**: a linear-time recurrent form for inference and a quadratic, matmul-friendly form used inside chunks for training.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} h_3 &= a_3a_2\,\Delta_1x_1B_1^\top + a_3\,\Delta_2x_2B_2^\top + \Delta_3x_3B_3^\top \\ y_3 = h_3C_3 &= \underbrace{a_3a_2}_{L_{31}}(B_1^\top C_3)\,\Delta_1x_1 + \underbrace{a_3}_{L_{32}}(B_2^\top C_3)\,\Delta_2x_2 + \underbrace{1}_{L_{33}}(B_3^\top C_3)\,\Delta_3x_3 \end{aligned}
blocks.caption: Three steps of the recurrence unrolled from h_0 = 0, leaving out the D skip. Each term is one earlier write, shrunk by every decay applied since.

blocks.md:
Here is the unrolling step by step. Start from $h_0 = 0$. Step 1 writes $\Delta_1x_1B_1^\top$. Step 2 multiplies that by $a_2$ and adds its own write. Step 3 multiplies everything by $a_3$ and adds a third write, which is the first line above. Reading with $C_3$ turns each outer product $x_jB_j^\top$ into $x_j$ times the single number $B_j^\top C_3$, a query-key score. The factor in front of each term is row 3 of the mask $L$ defined next: $L_{31} = a_3a_2$, $L_{32} = a_3$, $L_{33} = 1$.

Check it on the toy head above. Token 3 reads with $C_3 = (1, 0)$, so only token 1's write (with $B_1 = (1, 0)$) scores 1, and $y_3 = a_3a_2 \cdot 1 \cdot \Delta_1x_1 = 0.905 \times 0.607 \times 0.5 = 0.274$, the value the trace printed.

blocks.tex: Y = \big(L \circ C B^\top\big) X, \qquad L_{ij} = \begin{cases} a_i \, a_{i-1} \cdots a_{j+1} & i \ge j \\ 0 & i < j \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Dual (quadratic) form of SSD, with each row x_j of X already scaled by its step size dt_j (the factor in the recurrence above). With every a_t = 1, L is the plain causal mask and the layer is ordinary causal linear attention.

blocks.md: In words: output $i$ adds up, over every earlier position $j$, the query-key score $C_i^\top B_j$, times the product of the decays $a_{j+1}$ through $a_i$, times $x_j$. That product is exactly how much token $j$'s write has shrunk by the time step $i$ reads the state, so the mask $L$ plays the role the decay plays in the recurrence. Building the full matrix, one row and one column per token, costs work that grows with the square of the length, which is why it is used only inside short chunks: as in the chunkwise form from the linear attention course, each chunk builds its own small $L$ and multiplies it out, while the state $h$ carries everything earlier from one chunk to the next.

blocks.title: The decay mask L for 5 tokens

scenes.caption: All a_t = 1: L is the causal mask, so every past token counts fully. This is causal linear attention.
All a_t = 0.9: weight fades geometrically with distance, 0.656 for t0 as seen from t4. Older tokens matter less.
Selective: token t3 has a large step so a_3 = 0.1. Everything before t3 is scaled by 0.1 instead of 0.9 in all later rows (0.073 instead of 0.656 for t0 at t4). The model chose to forget.

blocks.md: **The short convolution.** Before the SSM, a Mamba-2 layer passes $x$, $B$ and $C$ through a depthwise causal convolution of width 4 (`d_conv=4` in mamba_ssm). Depthwise means each channel is mixed only with its own past: channel c at token t becomes a learned weighted sum of channel c at tokens t-3 to t. Causal means it never looks ahead. So before anything enters the state, each token's vectors already depend on its few neighbors, not just on itself. The next lesson's lab relies on exactly this: a value token's key-like vector must carry the key token just before it. It is also why the cache keeps the last few inputs: the next token's convolution needs them.

**Mamba-1 versus Mamba-2.** Jamba uses the original Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023). There, each channel of x runs its own SSM, a head dimension of 1: $A$ is a diagonal matrix with N decay rates per channel, the step size $\Delta$ is computed per channel and per token, and $B$ and $C$ (N numbers each) are computed from the token and shared by all channels. Mamba-1 computes this with a hardware-aware scan kernel, a parallel prefix-style pass over the sequence. Mamba-2 restricts $A$ to one scalar per head and uses heads of P = 64 or 128 channels. Its paper calls this a slight loss of expressive power in return for training efficiency: with one decay per head the mask $L$ is shared by the whole head, so the work inside a chunk becomes matrix multiplications that run on the graphics processing unit's (GPU's) tensor cores, its matrix-multiply units.

For the cache, what matters is the recurrent form. A Mamba-2 layer stores, per sequence, the state $h$ for every head plus a short convolution buffer holding the last few inputs (window 4). In Nemotron-H-8B a layer has 128 heads of dimension 64 and state size 128, so $128 \times 64 \times 128 = 1{,}048{,}576$ numbers, whether the context is 10 tokens or 1 million.

The paper also reports that a dedicated SSD kernel is 2 to 8 times faster than Mamba-1's fused scan kernel and overtakes FlashAttention-2 (a fast exact softmax attention kernel that works on tiles and never stores the full score matrix) from about 2K tokens.

The duality does not make Mamba-2 as good at recall as softmax attention. The quadratic form is a way to compute the same layer faster in training; at inference, all past information still has to pass through the fixed state, and there is no softmax to pick one token sharply.

blocks.question: In a Mamba-2 head, the model sees a token that marks the start of an unrelated document. What setting lets the head discard the old context?
options: A small step size dt, so a stays near 1
A large step size dt, so a falls toward 0
Setting C to zero for that token
Increasing the state size N for that token
blocks.explain: a = exp(dt A) with A negative. A large dt drives a toward 0, which multiplies the whole state by a small number. C only affects what is read, and N is fixed by the architecture.

blocks.question: During decoding at 100K tokens of context, which part of a Mamba-2 layer's per-sequence memory grows with the context?
options: The SSM state h
The convolution buffer
Both, linearly in context length
Neither; both have fixed size
blocks.explain: Both the state (heads x head dim x N) and the convolution window (4 inputs) are fixed by the architecture. That fixed size is exactly why hybrids use these layers, and also why they cannot store unlimited exact detail.

lessons.title: Measure recall yourself: MQAR and a tiny hybrid in code

blocks.md:
The first lesson argued the recall gap from a formula and from published benchmarks. Here you run the experiment the field uses to compare sequence mixers. As the previous course showed, Zoology (Arora et al., 2023) traced most of the perplexity gap between attention and attention-free models to **associative recall**: predicting a token by looking up a pair stated earlier in the context. They formalized it as **multi-query associative recall (MQAR)**: the input lists key-value pairs, and later the keys reappear, each time asking for its value. Their example is `A 4 B 3 C 6 F 1 E 2` followed by queries `A ? C ? F ? E ? B ?`, whose answers are 4, 6, 1, 2, 3.

The word that matters is *multi*. Older recall tests asked one question at the end, so a model could get by remembering a little. With many queries at different distances, every pair has to stay retrievable at once.

blocks.title: One MQAR sequence with 3 pairs (our layout)

scenes.caption: First the D = 3 pairs: keys A, B, C, each followed by its value. Nothing is scored here; the model only has to store them.
Then the keys come back in a new order. At each repeated key the model must output that key's value: 6 after C, 4 after A, 3 after B.
Attention can find the earlier C and copy what followed it. A recurrent layer must have kept all 3 pairs in its fixed state, because it cannot know which key will be asked first.

blocks.md:
Our version is simpler than Zoology's: all D pairs come first, then all D keys again in a shuffled order, each followed by its value, so a sequence has 4D tokens. Zoology instead places the second occurrences at distances drawn from a power law and fills gaps with other tokens. The vocabulary has 128 key tokens and 128 value tokens, and the loss counts only the positions right after a repeated key.

The recurrent mixer is the gated linear attention you know, in Mamba-2's scalar-decay form: state $S_t = a_tS_{t-1} + v_tk_t^\top$, output $S_tq_t$, with one decay $a_t$ per token. We drop Mamba-2's step-size scaling of the write to keep the code short. Training uses the dual form from the previous lesson, so the first snippet checks it against the plain loop.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
V, KEYS = 256, 128               # tokens 0-127 are keys, 128-255 values

def mqar_batch(B, D):            # D pairs, then the D keys again, shuffled
    k = torch.stack([torch.randperm(KEYS)[:D] for _ in range(B)])
    v = torch.randint(KEYS, V, (B, D))
    perm = torch.stack([torch.randperm(D) for _ in range(B)])
    kq, vq = k.gather(1, perm), v.gather(1, perm)
    x = torch.cat([torch.stack([k, v], -1).flatten(1),
                   torch.stack([kq, vq], -1).flatten(1)], 1)
    y = torch.full_like(x, -100)  # -100 = no loss at this position
    y[:, 2 * D::2] = vq           # at each repeated key, predict its value
    return x, y

def gla_loop(q, k, v, a):        # q, k: [T, N]  v: [T, P]  a: [T]
    S, out = torch.zeros(v.shape[1], k.shape[1]), []
    for t in range(len(a)):
        S = a[t] * S + torch.outer(v[t], k[t])   # decay, then write
        out.append(S @ q[t])                     # read
    return torch.stack(out)

def gla_parallel(q, k, v, loga): # same layer, dual form: (L o QK^T) V
    c = loga.cumsum(-1)
    diff = c[..., :, None] - c[..., None, :]     # log(a_{j+1} ... a_i)
    causal = torch.ones_like(diff, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
    L = torch.exp(diff.masked_fill(~causal, -torch.inf))
    return ((q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)) * L) @ v

torch.manual_seed(1)
q, k, v, a = torch.randn(7, 3), torch.randn(7, 3), torch.randn(7, 2), torch.rand(7)
print((gla_loop(q, k, v, a) - gla_parallel(q, k, v, a.log())).abs().max())
blocks.caption: Data and the recurrent mixer. Output on CPU: tensor(3.2783e-07), so the loop and the masked matrix form agree to float32 rounding. The mask is built in log space and set to minus infinity above the diagonal before exp, which avoids overflow and NaN gradients on long sequences.

blocks.code:
class Mixer(nn.Module):          # "rec": Mamba-2-style layer, "attn": softmax
    def __init__(self, kind, d, N):
        super().__init__()
        self.kind, self.N = kind, N
        self.conv = nn.Conv1d(d, d, 4, groups=d, padding=3)  # short causal conv
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d, 2 * N + d + 1 if kind == "rec" else 3 * d)
        self.norm, self.out = nn.RMSNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, d)

    def forward(self, x):        # x: [batch, T, d]
        T = x.shape[1]
        x = self.conv(x.transpose(1, 2))[..., :T].transpose(1, 2)
        if self.kind == "rec":
            q, k, v, dt = self.proj(x).split([self.N, self.N, x.shape[-1], 1], -1)
            loga = -F.softplus(dt.squeeze(-1))   # a = exp(-softplus(dt)), in (0, 1)
            y = self.norm(gla_parallel(q, F.normalize(k, dim=-1), v, loga))
        else:
            q, k, v = self.proj(x).chunk(3, -1)
            y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
        return self.out(y)
blocks.caption: One mixer layer. Both kinds start with the same width-4 causal convolution. The recurrent kind has an N-dimensional key, so its state is a d x N = 64 x N matrix per layer. The attention kind is one head with no position embedding. nn.RMSNorm needs PyTorch 2.4 or later.

blocks.code:
class Model(nn.Module):          # kinds: e.g. ["rec", "attn"]
    def __init__(self, kinds, d=64, N=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(V, d)
        self.mix = nn.ModuleList(Mixer(k, d, N) for k in kinds)
        self.mlp = nn.ModuleList(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(),
                                               nn.Linear(4 * d, d)) for _ in kinds)
        self.n1 = nn.ModuleList(nn.LayerNorm(d) for _ in kinds)
        self.n2 = nn.ModuleList(nn.LayerNorm(d) for _ in kinds)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d, V)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.emb(x)
        for m, f, a, b in zip(self.mix, self.mlp, self.n1, self.n2):
            h = h + m(a(h))
            h = h + f(b(h))
        return self.head(h)

def run(kinds, D, steps=2000, lr=3e-3, N=16, B=64):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = Model(kinds, N=N)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.1)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, lr, total_steps=steps)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x, y = mqar_batch(B, D)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x).flatten(0, 1), y.flatten())
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); sched.step()
    with torch.no_grad():        # accuracy on 512 fresh sequences
        x, y = mqar_batch(512, D)
        m = y != -100
        return (model(x).argmax(-1)[m] == y[m]).float().mean().item()
blocks.caption: A 2-layer model (mixer then MLP, each with a residual connection and LayerNorm) and the training loop. run(['rec', 'attn'], D=16) trains the hybrid on 16 pairs and returns recall accuracy.

blocks.md:
The experiment: four 2-layer models, width d = 64, trained for 2,000 steps of 64 sequences each at D = 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 pairs:

- **attn + attn**: two attention layers.
- **rec + rec, N = 16**: two recurrent layers with a 64 x 16 state (1,024 numbers each).
- **rec + rec, N = 64**: the same with a 64 x 64 state (4,096 numbers).
- **rec + attn, N = 16**: a recurrent layer, then one attention layer.

Recurrent models are harder to train on MQAR, so, like Zoology (which sweeps four rates), each model is trained at three learning rates (0.001, 0.003, 0.01) and the best accuracy is reported. Each point is one seed. The whole grid ran on a laptop CPU in under an hour, eight single-thread runs at a time.

blocks.prompt: Before looking: the N = 16 recurrent model has a state with 16 key directions. What happens to its accuracy as the number of pairs goes from 4 to 64, and what does one attention layer change?
blocks.reveal: With 16 key directions the recurrent model is near perfect at 4 and 8 pairs, about half right at 16 (49.4%), and at chance from 32 pairs up: 0.9% and 0.8%, about one in 128, the number of possible values. A 64-dimensional key keeps 16 pairs at 99.6% but still fails at 32 and 64 within the same 2,000 steps. One attention layer on top of the N = 16 recurrent layer recalls every pair at every size, exactly like two attention layers.

blocks.title: MQAR recall accuracy by number of pairs (our runs)

scenes.caption: Two attention layers: 100% at every size from 4 to 64 pairs (best of three learning rates). A lookup does not care how many pairs are stored.
Two recurrent layers with N = 16: 100% and 99.2% at 4 and 8 pairs, 49.4% at 16, then 0.9% and 0.8% at 32 and 64 pairs, which is chance (1 in 128).
The same model with N = 64: 99.6% at 16 pairs, so the bigger state moves the cliff to the right, but 32 and 64 pairs are still at chance after 2,000 steps.
A recurrent layer (N = 16) then one attention layer: 100% at every size, the same as pure attention. One lookup layer restores recall.

blocks.md: Tie this back to the first lesson's formula. Each recurrent state is a d x N matrix read with N-dimensional keys, so crosstalk grows like pairs over N: with N = 16 the cosine estimate is 0.72 at 16 pairs and 0.45 at 64. How far a 2-layer toy gets also depends on training, and the collapse at 32 pairs is partly optimization. In one extra run outside the grid (one seed, 32 pairs, 6,000 steps instead of 2,000, learning rates 0.001 and 0.003), the N = 64 model reached 94.4% at 0.001 but stayed at chance at 0.003, and the N = 16 model stayed at chance at both rates. A single run is weak evidence, but it suggests that the state size, not only the training budget, sets where recall breaks; attention, which compresses nothing, never broke.

What the toy shows: with a fixed state, recall falls once the pairs outnumber what the state can hold cleanly, a bigger state moves that point, and one attention layer restores it. What it does not show: real scale. These are 2-layer models, one seed each, the curves depend on the learning rate, and the task is synthetic. At scale, Zoology measured the same pattern on the Pile (a large open text collection used for pretraining), and the first lesson's phone-book results show it for 8B models.

There is also a proof that no training trick removes the limit. Jelassi et al. ([Repeat After Me](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01032), 2024) show that a model with a fixed-size state cannot copy strings that carry more bits than the state holds, while a two-layer Transformer can copy strings whose length is exponential in its number of heads. The previous course works through that counting bound; here the point is the engineering consequence: to keep exact recall at any length, keep some attention.

blocks.question: Why does MQAR separate a recurrent model from attention more sharply than a test with a single query at the end?
options: A single query lets the model store little; with many queries at different times, every pair must stay retrievable at once
MQAR sequences are much longer, and recurrent models cannot run on long sequences
MQAR uses a larger vocabulary, which recurrent models cannot embed
With one query, attention cannot find the key
blocks.explain: With one question at the end, a recurrent model can in principle get by with whatever survived in its state. MQAR asks about every pair, in an order the model cannot predict, so all of them must be held simultaneously in the fixed state. Attention just looks each one up.

blocks.question: In the lab, which change rescued recall at 32 pairs for the N = 16 model within the same 2,000 training steps?
options: Training the N = 16 recurrent model three times longer
Replacing its second recurrent layer with one attention layer
Raising the learning rate to 0.01
Removing the short convolution to simplify the layer
blocks.explain: The recurrent-then-attention model scored 100% at 32 and 64 pairs. In our one longer run, the N = 16 model was still at chance after 6,000 steps, and 0.01 was one of the three rates already tried. The convolution is what lets a value token carry the key before it, so removing it takes information away rather than adding capacity.

lessons.title: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers

blocks.md:
A hybrid is defined by its **layer pattern**: which layers mix tokens with attention, which with an SSM, and where the MLPs (or mixture-of-experts layers) go. AI21's **Jamba** (2024), which its authors call the first production-grade attention-SSM hybrid, is the classic example. It repeats a **Jamba block** of $l = 8$ layers with an attention-to-Mamba ratio $a{:}m = 1{:}7$. Each layer is a mixer (attention or Mamba) followed by an MLP, and every $e = 2$ layers that MLP is a **mixture of experts** (MoE) with $n = 16$ experts, of which the top $K = 2$ run per token.

Four such blocks give 32 layers: 52B total parameters, 12B active per token.

Two details in the figure below. Each layer is wrapped in a residual connection (its output is added to its input) and an RMSNorm, root mean square normalization: divide the vector by the root mean square of its entries, then multiply by a learned gain per dimension, which keeps activations at a steady scale. And Transformers usually tell attention where each token sits with rotary position embedding (RoPE), which rotates every query and key by angles proportional to the token's position, so a query-key score depends on how far apart the two tokens are.

blocks.title: One Jamba block (8 layers)

scenes.caption: Eight layers in order. Each is a sequence mixer followed by an MLP, with RMSNorm and residual connections (not drawn).
Only layer 4 uses attention, matching the released config (attn_layer_offset 4, period 8). Over 32 layers that is 4 attention layers, so the KV cache is 8x smaller than a same-depth Transformer.
Odd layers swap the MLP for a 16-expert MoE with top-2 routing. This raises total parameters (capacity) while keeping active parameters per token at 12B.
No RoPE anywhere: the paper found results with and without RoPE were similar, presumably because Mamba layers before attention provide position information implicitly.

blocks.md:
Why can a Mamba layer stand in for position embeddings? A recurrence reads tokens in order, and each write is shrunk by every later decay, so the same tokens in a different order leave a different state. Take one number of state with a fixed decay of 0.5, $h_t = 0.5\,h_{t-1} + x_t$. Reading 1 then 2 gives $0.5 \cdot 1 + 2 = 2.5$; reading 2 then 1 gives $0.5 \cdot 2 + 1 = 2.0$.

A single softmax attention layer without position embeddings has no such signal: its output is a softmax-weighted sum over the earlier keys and values, and a sum does not change when two of its terms swap places. So swapping two earlier tokens leaves a later token's attention output unchanged, unless the vectors themselves already carry order. In a hybrid they do, because the Mamba layers below have mixed order into every token's vector. (Stacked causal attention can also pick up some order without position embeddings, from the causal mask alone, as [Haviv et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16634) showed; Jamba cites this.)

NVIDIA took a different route. Instead of a repeated block, **Mamba-2-Hybrid 8B** (Waleffe et al., 2024) treats Mamba-2, attention and MLP as separate layers and spreads them evenly: 56 layers = 24 Mamba-2 + 4 attention + 28 MLP, with a Mamba-2 layer first and no position embeddings. **Nemotron-H** (2025) follows the same recipe with extra rules: the first layer is Mamba-2, the last is a feed-forward network (another name for the MLP), and every attention layer is followed by a feed-forward network. The released Nemotron-H-8B config encodes this as a 52-character pattern string.

blocks.title: Nemotron-H-8B layer pattern (M = Mamba-2, A = attention, F = FFN)

scenes.caption: All 52 layers from the config's hybrid_override_pattern. Mamba-2 and FFN layers alternate; attention appears only 4 times.
The 4 attention layers sit at indices 7, 18, 29 and 40, roughly evenly spaced, and each is followed by an FFN, as in a Transformer block.
24 Mamba-2 layers (46.2%) do most of the token mixing; they hold fixed-size state. 4 of 52 layers (7.7%) are attention, the only ones with a growing KV cache.
24 FFN layers (46.2%) mix nothing across tokens. The 56B model uses the same pattern stretched to 118 layers with 10 attention layers (8.5%).

blocks.md: Hybrids are not limited to Mamba. **Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B** (Alibaba Qwen, 2025) uses the Gated DeltaNet layer from the previous course. Its 48 layers follow the layout 12 x (3 x (Gated DeltaNet then MoE) then 1 x (Gated Attention then MoE)), so one layer in four keeps a KV cache. Gated Attention is softmax attention whose output is multiplied entry by entry by a sigmoid gate computed from the token, so each head can scale its output down toward zero when it has nothing useful (Qiu et al., 2025). The attention layers use 16 query heads, 2 KV heads and head dimension 256: this is grouped-query attention (GQA), where each group of 8 query heads shares one key head and one value head, so the cache stores 2 heads instead of 16, and the model card states a native context of 262,144 tokens.

blocks.title: Share of layers that are full attention

scenes.caption: Counting attention layers over all layers that mix tokens or apply an MLP: Jamba 4/32 = 12.5%, Mamba-2-Hybrid 4/56 = 7.1%, Nemotron-H 4/52 = 7.7% and 10/118 = 8.5%.

Counting per mixer instead (ignoring MLPs): Mamba-2-Hybrid and Nemotron-H-8B become 4 of 28 = 14.3%, Nemotron-H-56B 10 of 64 = 15.6%; Jamba and Qwen3-Next do not change. Always check which denominator a paper uses.

blocks.md: To read any hybrid's layout, open its config.json: Jamba uses attn_layer_period and attn_layer_offset, Nemotron-H uses hybrid_override_pattern, and Qwen3-Next uses full_attention_interval = 4.

blocks.question: Jamba-v0.1's config has 32 layers, attn_layer_period 8 and attn_layer_offset 4. Which layers (0-based) are attention?
blocks.explain: Attention sits where layer index mod 8 equals 4: layers 4, 12, 20 and 28. The other 28 layers are Mamba, giving the 1:7 ratio.

blocks.question: Why does Nemotron-H place a Mamba-2 layer first and use no RoPE in its attention layers?
options: RoPE is incompatible with grouped-query attention
The first Mamba-2 layer is recurrent and naturally encodes position, so explicit position embeddings are not needed
Attention layers at the start would make the KV cache grow quadratically
Mamba-2 layers require RoPE inputs and must come before attention
blocks.explain: Waleffe et al. put a Mamba layer at the start so the hybrid can work without position embeddings, since the recurrence itself depends on order. Their 840M ablation also found the hybrid without RoPE did better after long-context extension (continued training on longer sequences to raise the usable context).

lessons.title: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state

blocks.md: The memory win of a hybrid comes almost entirely from the KV cache. For each attention layer, every token stores one key and one value per KV head. Everything below assumes 16-bit (2-byte) numbers. Some deployments keep the SSM state itself in 32-bit because recurrent states are sensitive to precision (vLLM exposes this as `mamba_ssm_cache_dtype`); that doubles the state's bytes and roughly doubles the crossover length computed below.

blocks.tex: \text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times L_{\text{attn}} \times n_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times 2
blocks.caption: The first 2 is K and V; the last 2 is bytes per number. L_attn counts only attention layers.

blocks.md: Jamba's paper reports KV cache sizes at 256K tokens (262,144) and the formula reproduces them exactly. Llama-2 7B has 32 layers with 32 KV heads of dimension 128: 512 KiB per token, so 128 GiB at 256K. These are binary units: a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes, a mebibyte is 1,024 kibibytes, and a gibibyte is 1,024 mebibytes, about 1.07 billion bytes. Mistral 7B and Mixtral, its mixture-of-experts sibling, use grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads: 128 KiB per token, 32 GiB. Jamba keeps the 8 KV heads but has only 4 attention layers: 16 KiB per token, 4 GiB.

blocks.title: KV cache for one 256K-token sequence (16-bit)

scenes.caption: Full multi-head attention in all 32 layers: 128 GiB, more than a single 80 GB GPU holds.
GQA cuts KV heads from 32 to 8, a 4x saving: 32 GiB for both Mistral and Mixtral.
Replacing 28 of 32 attention layers with Mamba gives another 8x: 4 GiB. The Mamba layers add a fixed state that does not depend on context.

blocks.md:
Now a fair comparison. NVIDIA trained **Nemotron-T-8B**, a 32-layer Transformer, on exactly the same data as Nemotron-H-8B, with the same hidden size 4096 and GQA with 8 KV heads of dimension 128.

- Nemotron-T-8B: $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes = 128 KiB per token.
- Nemotron-H-8B: 4 attention layers, so 16 KiB per token.
- Plus the fixed Mamba-2 state, computed next.

blocks.caption: Per sequence, from the config: 24 Mamba-2 layers, 128 heads x head dim 64 x state 128, conv channels = inner dim 8192 plus B and C for 8 groups, window 4.

blocks.md: In words: each of the 24 Mamba-2 layers keeps $128 \times 64 \times 128 = 1{,}048{,}576$ state numbers, plus a convolution buffer with the last 4 inputs of its 10,240 channels (8,192 inner channels plus $B$ and $C$, each 8 groups of 128), which is 40,960 numbers. At 2 bytes each that is about 49.9 MiB per sequence. The Transformer stores $128 - 16 = 112$ KiB more per token than the hybrid, so the fixed state is paid back after 49.9 MiB divided by 112 KiB, about 456 tokens: the crossover in the next figure.

blocks.title: Cache memory per sequence: Nemotron-T-8B vs Nemotron-H-8B

scenes.caption: Below about 456 tokens the hybrid uses more cache memory: its 49.9 MiB of fixed state outweighs the extra KV of the Transformer. Fixed cost, small slope.
At 64K tokens: 8 GiB for the Transformer vs 1.05 GiB for the hybrid, a 7.6x reduction. As context grows the ratio approaches 32/4 = 8x.
Drag a: with 16 attention layers the hybrid's slope is half the Transformer's. The KV saving is set by how few attention layers you keep.

blocks.prompt: Simplified model: after weights, 40 GiB of GPU memory is left for caches. How many 64K-token sequences fit for Nemotron-T-8B, and how many for Nemotron-H-8B?
blocks.reveal: Transformer: 8 GiB each, so **5** sequences. Hybrid: about 1.05 GiB each, so **38** sequences. Larger batches are where much of the throughput gain comes from. Simplified: real servers also need activation memory and allocate cache in blocks.

blocks.md: Compute follows the same shape. When decoding, each attention layer reads all $T$ cached tokens, while a Mamba-2 layer does a fixed amount of work. Waleffe et al. predicted their 8B hybrid would generate tokens nearly 8x faster than the Transformer at long contexts (batch 32). Measured end to end, Nemotron-H-8B was 1.8x and 3x faster than Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B with 65,536 input and 1,024 output tokens on NVIDIA H100 graphics processing units, and Jamba reached 3x Mixtral's throughput at 128K tokens.

blocks.caption: Decode FLOPs (floating-point operations) per token. T is the context length and d = 32 query heads x 128 = 4,096. A Mamba-2 layer touches each of its H x P x N state numbers about five times (decay, outer-product write, add, read).

blocks.md: Put numbers in at T = 65,536. One attention layer: $4 \times 65{,}536 \times 4{,}096 \approx 1.07$ billion FLOPs, so the Transformer's 32 layers spend 34.4 GFLOPs per token on attention. One Mamba-2 layer: about $5 \times 1{,}048{,}576 \approx 5.2$ million FLOPs. The weights cost about 2 FLOPs per parameter, roughly 16 GFLOPs for 8B parameters, the same in both models. Totals: about 50.4 GFLOPs per token for the Transformer and 16 + 4.3 + 0.13, about 20.4, for the hybrid, a 2.5x gap. At 8K tokens it is only 20.3 vs 16.7, 1.2x. So at moderate context the weight matmuls dominate, and arithmetic alone cannot produce an 8x speedup.

Decoding is usually limited by memory traffic, not arithmetic: each step reads every weight once (shared by the whole batch) plus every sequence's cache. In a simplified model with 16 GB of 16-bit weights, at batch 32 and 64K tokens the Transformer reads 291 GB per step and the hybrid 52 GB, a 5.6x gap that approaches $32/4 = 8$x as context grows. That is the regime of the predicted 8x (batch 32, long inputs). The measured 1.8x and 3x compare against other models: Qwen-2.5-7B has 28 layers with 4 KV heads of dimension 128, 56 KiB per token ([config](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B/blob/main/config.json)), while Llama-3.1-8B has 32 layers with 8 KV heads, 128 KiB per token ([Llama 3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)). Against a cache less than half as large, a smaller speedup is what the model predicts.

blocks.title: Bytes read per decode step (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Batch 1: weights (16 GB) dominate. At 64K the Transformer reads 24.6 GB and the hybrid 17.1 GB, only 1.44x. Simplified: real engines also read activations and differ in kernels.
Batch 32: the caches dominate. At 64K, 290.9 vs 52.0 GB (5.6x); at 128K, 565.8 vs 86.4 GB (6.5x), heading toward 8x.

blocks.md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

blocks.question: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B has 12 full attention layers, each with 2 KV heads of dimension 256. How much KV cache does one token need in 16-bit?
options: 6 KiB
12 KiB
192 KiB
24 KiB
blocks.explain: 2 (K and V) x 12 layers x 2 heads x 256 x 2 bytes = 24,576 bytes = 24 KiB. At 262,144 tokens that is 6 GiB, plus the fixed Gated DeltaNet state of the other 36 layers.

blocks.question: An engineer replaces 28 of 32 attention layers with Mamba-2 and is surprised the cache barely shrinks in their chatbot with 300-token conversations. Why?
options: Mamba-2 layers keep a KV cache too
Below the crossover length, the fixed SSM state is as large as or larger than the KV cache it replaced
GQA already removed all KV memory
The KV cache only matters during training
blocks.explain: For Nemotron-H-8B-like sizes the fixed state is about 50 MiB per sequence, as much as about 400 tokens of the Transformer's 128 KiB per token. With the hybrid's own 16 KiB per token added, the two break even at 456 tokens. Short conversations sit below that crossover, so the hybrid's advantage appears only at longer contexts.

lessons.title: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill

blocks.md:
The previous course ended with one serving fact: a recurrent state can only be reused as a whole snapshot, and vLLM saves Mamba-style states at block boundaries. This lesson follows that fact through an inference server.

A tiny example sets the scene. Three chat requests start with the same 2,000-token system prompt, then each adds its own question. A server with **prefix caching** computes the shared 2,000 tokens once and reuses the result for the other two requests, which cuts their time to first token (the delay before the first output token appears).

For a hybrid this is harder. An attention layer's cache for 2,500 tokens contains the cache for its first 2,000: the keys and values of positions 1 to 2,000 are simply its first 2,000 entries, so any prefix can be kept or shared. A Mamba layer's state after 2,500 tokens is one fixed-size tensor that was overwritten in place 2,500 times, and the last 500 tokens cannot be subtracted back out.

The Marconi paper (Pan et al.) names three properties behind the trouble: SSM states have a fixed size however many tokens they summarize; they are updated in place, so they cannot be rolled back to represent a prefix; and they are far larger than one token's KV entries. Reuse becomes all or nothing: a hit needs, for every Mamba layer, a state saved at exactly the position where the reuse ends.

Count the bytes for the shared 2,000-token prompt with Nemotron-H-8B: 16 KiB of KV per token and 49.9 MiB per full set of Mamba-2 states and convolution buffers, from the cache lesson.

- KV for the 4 attention layers: 2,000 x 16 KiB = 31.25 MiB, reusable at any block boundary.
- A state snapshot every 16 tokens, so a hit can land on any 16-token block: 125 snapshots, 6,234 MiB, about 6.1 GiB, for one prompt.
- A snapshot every 512 tokens: 3 snapshots (at 512, 1,024 and 1,536), 150 MiB. A new request resumes at token 1,536 and recomputes 464 tokens.
- One snapshot exactly at token 2,000: 49.9 MiB and nothing to recompute, but only if the server knows where the shared part ends.

For comparison, Nemotron-T-8B keeps 2,000 x 128 KiB = 250 MiB of KV and needs no snapshot.

blocks.title: Cache for one shared 2,000-token prompt

scenes.caption: Snapshotting the state at every 16-token block costs about 6 GiB for a single prompt, roughly 200x the KV it accompanies.
Without the fine-grained option: one well-placed snapshot plus the hybrid's KV (81 MiB) is a third of the Transformer's 250 MiB of KV for the same prefix.

blocks.md:
Marconi's answer is to admit few states and evict carefully. It records request history in a radix tree (a prefix tree whose edges hold runs of tokens). Before prefilling a request it does a speculative insertion: if the new prompt would split an existing edge, the split point is a prefix shared by at least two requests, so the server saves the SSM states there during this prefill. It also always saves the state after the last decoded token, because a chat's next turn appends to it.

For eviction it scores entries by recency plus **FLOP efficiency**: the compute a hit would save divided by the bytes the entry holds. An SSM state has a fixed size while the compute it saves grows with the prefix length, so long prefixes score high. With 32-token checkpoints the paper measured that 25.0% of KV blocks but only 0.4% of SSM states were ever reused; Marconi reports up to 34.4x higher token hit rates than a vLLM-based baseline that checkpoints states at every block.

blocks.question: A server snapshots SSM states only at branch points found by Marconi-style speculative insertion, plus after each request's last decoded token. A new system prompt appears in requests 1, 2 and 3, each with a different question. Which is the first request whose Mamba layers can reuse the prompt?
options: Request 1
Request 2
Request 3
None of them, since recurrent states cannot be shared
blocks.explain: Request 1 creates the tree entry; nothing is shared yet. Request 2's insertion splits that edge at the end of the shared prompt, so its prefill saves the states there. Request 3 is the first to hit them. The paper accepts missing the second occurrence because hot prefixes are shared by many requests.

blocks.md:
**Speculative decoding** lets a small draft model propose K tokens, then runs the large model once over all K to verify them; the longest prefix the large model agrees with is kept and the rest thrown away. For attention, throwing tokens away means dropping their KV entries. A recurrent layer that processed all K drafts has already overwritten its state, so the state at the last accepted token is gone.

There are two fixes: store the state after every draft token (K full snapshots per sequence), or keep the state from before the drafts and recompute through the accepted ones. Mamba in the Llama (Wang, Paliotta et al., 2024) does the second with a fused multi-step kernel that, starting from a cached state, produces the outputs for the drafts and returns both the state at the last verified position and the final state, so only one state stays cached. In a hybrid the attention layers verify in parallel as usual. On H100 GPUs a naive multi-kernel version gave no speedup; the fused one reached about 2x for a Mamba 7B verifier drafting 4 tokens with a Llama-3 1B draft model.

blocks.title: Rejecting draft tokens: KV truncates, the state must be restored

scenes.caption: Tokens 1 to 4 are verified. The attention layers hold 4 KV entries; each Mamba layer holds one state, h4, which summarizes all four.
The draft proposes d5 to d8 and one verifier pass reads all four. Attention appends 4 entries. The state is overwritten to h8, so h4 survives only if it was kept aside.
The verifier agrees with d5 and d6 but not d7, so it keeps 2 drafts and emits its own token at position 7. Attention just truncates to 6 entries.
h8 includes the rejected d7 and d8 and cannot be trimmed. Restore from h4 and recompute through d5 and d6 to get h6 (the multi-step kernel returns it directly), then continue from h6.

blocks.md: **Chunked prefill** splits a long prompt into pieces and schedules them alongside other requests' decode steps, so one long prompt does not stall everyone; vLLM enables it by default and chunks any prefill that does not fit its per-step token budget ([docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization.html)). For the attention layers, each chunk attends to the KV entries of earlier chunks. For the Mamba layers it is the chunkwise training algorithm stretched across scheduler steps: start the chunk from the state the previous chunk left, and hand the new state on. The reference kernel exposes this directly: `mamba_chunk_scan_combined` takes `initial_states` and can return the final states ([source](https://github.com/state-spaces/mamba/blob/main/mamba_ssm/ops/triton/ssd_combined.py)). Chunk boundaries are also cheap places to snapshot: Marconi saves the state at the last chunk boundary inside a prefix (with 32-token chunks, a prefix ending at token 80 is checkpointed at 64) and recomputes the rest.

**Memory planning.** Each running sequence needs one state slot per Mamba layer, the same size for every request, so the state memory for N concurrent requests is known up front; only the attention layers need paged blocks that grow. Mixing the two in one memory pool takes care. vLLM uses a single page size for all layer types, so it raises the attention block size until one block of one attention layer's KV is at least as large as one Mamba layer's state, and pads the state to that size. For Nemotron-H-8B with a 16-bit state, a Mamba-2 layer's state plus convolution buffer is 2,158,592 bytes (vLLM keeps the last 3 convolution inputs, not 4) and one token of one attention layer's KV is 4,096 bytes, so a block would need at least 527 tokens, rounded up to the kernel's block alignment. vLLM's design doc notes this can push attention blocks past 400 tokens, which it calls too large ([design doc](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/hybrid_kv_cache_manager.html)). Coarse blocks also mean coarser prefix-cache hits, the checkpoint trade-off from above.

A recurrent state is compact but not divisible. Every serving feature that cuts a cache at an arbitrary token (sharing a prefix, rejecting speculative tokens, pausing a prefill) needs a saved state at that exact position or a recomputation from an earlier one. Plan where states are checkpointed the way you plan KV memory.

blocks.question: A hybrid serves with speculative decoding and 4 draft tokens. The verifier accepts the first 2 drafts and rejects the third. What has to happen in the Mamba layers?
options: Truncate the state to drop the rejected drafts, as with the KV cache
Nothing: the state forgets the rejected drafts within a few tokens
Recompute the whole prompt from token 1
Restore a state saved before the drafts and recompute through the 2 accepted drafts
blocks.explain: The state after the verifier pass includes all 4 drafts and cannot be trimmed. Restoring the pre-draft state and recomputing 2 tokens is cheap; Mamba in the Llama fuses this into its multi-step kernel. Decay does not erase rejected tokens reliably, and recomputing the whole prompt throws away the cache.

blocks.question: A hybrid's Mamba layer state is 1 MiB and one token of one attention layer's KV is 2 KiB. Under vLLM's rule that one attention block must hold at least one Mamba state's bytes, what is the smallest attention block size?
options: 16 tokens
256 tokens
512 tokens
1,024 tokens
blocks.explain: 1 MiB is 1,048,576 bytes; divided by 2,048 bytes per token that is 512 tokens. Blocks that large make prefix-cache hits coarse, which is why vLLM's design doc calls 400-plus-token blocks too large.

lessons.title: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short

blocks.md: How much attention should a hybrid keep? The Mamba-2 paper trained 350M-parameter, 48-layer models on 7B tokens of the Pile (an 825 GiB open English text collection from EleutherAI, built from 22 sources such as web pages, books, papers and code), changing only how many of the 48 layers were attention. Everything else, including parameter count and data, was held fixed. The pure-attention baseline is Transformer++, the Mamba authors' name for a Transformer built with the modern LLaMA-style recipe: rotary position embedding, a gated multilayer perceptron, RMSNorm and no bias terms.

blocks.prompt: Pure Mamba-2 scored perplexity 8.60 and a pure Transformer++ 8.68. If 6 attention layers out of 48 helps, would 24 out of 48 help even more?
blocks.reveal: No. Perplexity is best around 6 attention layers (8.26) and gets worse with more: 24 attention layers give 8.50, close to the pure models. The authors conclude that **around 10%** attention works best. Jamba saw the same flatness: 1:3 and 1:7 ratios scored the same at 1.3B, so AI21 chose the cheaper 1:7.

blocks.title: Perplexity above the best mix (8.26), 350M model, 48 layers

scenes.caption: The two pure models: Mamba-2 is 0.34 above the best hybrid, Transformer++ 0.42 above. Neither layer type alone wins.
A single attention layer removes most of the gap (0.12). By 4 to 6 layers, about 8 to 12% of the stack, the curve is flat at its minimum.
Past that point, more attention hurts: 24 attention layers are 0.24 worse. More attention also means more KV cache, so it loses on both axes.

blocks.md:
Other ablations agree on the main rules:

- **Ratio**: Waleffe et al. found validation loss minimized at roughly 8% attention for 130M models (confirmed at 840M), and that 30% to 50% of layers can be MLPs with no loss increase; 50% MLPs trained 20% faster than 5%.
- **Placement**: spread attention layers out. Mamba-2's authors saw little dependence on exact position as long as attention is not at the very beginning or end; NVIDIA found no pattern better than evenly spaced.
- **Order**: put an SSM layer first so no position embedding is needed.
- **Stability**: Jamba hit large loss spikes (sudden jumps in training loss) at its 7B-based scale from big activations inside Mamba layers, fixed by adding RMSNorm to internal activations.

blocks.title: Four ways to give an SSM model exact recall

scenes.caption: Sequential interleaving: a few full attention layers among many SSM layers. Global exact recall, KV cache in only about 8% to 12% of layers.
Samba (Microsoft) pairs Mamba with sliding window attention of 2048 tokens: constant memory overall, but attention can only see the last window, so exact recall beyond it relies on the Mamba state.

Hymba (NVIDIA) runs attention and SSM heads in parallel inside each layer, then normalizes, rescales and averages them. Only the first, middle and last layers use global attention; the rest use sliding windows.
Qwen3-Next uses Gated DeltaNet instead of Mamba, with one gated attention layer every 4 layers. The recipe is the same: cheap fixed-state mixers plus periodic exact lookup.

blocks.md: The NVIDIA study also trained versions of the hybrid and the Transformer further on long documents so they handle 16K and 32K tokens. Multi-document question answering hands the model several retrieved passages, only some of which hold the answer; the rest are distractors. MuSiQue, short for multihop questions via single-hop question composition (Trivedi et al., 2022), is one such test: each question needs 2 to 4 facts combined from different paragraphs, mixed with distractor paragraphs.

Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on MuSiQue the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

**Extending a hybrid to long context.** A model pretrained on 4K-token sequences is usually extended by continued pretraining on longer ones. Waleffe et al. trained their 8B hybrid and Transformer for 50B more tokens at 16K and 32K, built by packing shorter documents together. The Transformer also needed its RoPE base frequency rescaled for the longer range (dynamic NTK scaling), while the hybrid's four attention layers have no position embedding to adjust. AI21 gave Jamba-1.5 a short mid-training phase with a high share of long documents. NVIDIA tuned its Nemotron-H reasoning models on conversations concatenated up to 512K tokens and reports that hybrids learn the longer context within a few hundred steps, reaching 83% on RULER at 128K.

**Evaluating it: RULER.** A single needle in a haystack (one fact hidden in filler text) is easy for hybrids and even for pure SSMs. RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), an NVIDIA benchmark, has 13 synthetic tasks in four groups: retrieval (eight needle variants, including multi-key with distractor needles, multi-value, and multi-query, which is MQAR at long range), multi-hop tracing (variable tracking: follow a chain like X2 = X1, X3 = X2 and list every name bound to a value), aggregation (return the most common or most frequent words) and question answering with distractor paragraphs. A model's effective length is the longest context at which its average stays above Llama-2-7B's 4K score of 85.6. Jamba-1.5-Large reports 93.9 at 256K, so its effective length equals its claimed 256K.

blocks.title: RULER tasks, NVIDIA 8B models (Waleffe et al., Table 10)

scenes.caption: Pure Mamba-2 at 4K: perfect on the single needle, 5.5 on multi-key 3 (a haystack made of distractor needles), 35 on multi-value. Many similar keys overload the state.
Transformer at 4K: 58 on multi-key 3, mid-90s on multi-value and multi-query.
Mamba-2-Hybrid at 4K: four attention layers lift multi-key 3 to 96 and multi-query to 97.6, above the Transformer.
32K extensions, Transformer: multi-key 3 falls to 41.25, and variable tracking to 0.35 because it copied the in-context example's answer.
32K extensions, hybrid: 81.5 on multi-key 3 and 79.9 on variable tracking. Aggregation (common words) is hard for both at 32K.

blocks.md: Read across the scenes. The single needle scores 100 for every model, so it cannot rank them. Tasks that load the context with many similar keys (multi-key with a haystack of distractor needles, multi-value, multi-query) separate pure Mamba-2 from the rest, and four attention layers close that gap, which is the MQAR result from the lab at real scale. Aggregation over the whole context stays hard for everyone at 32K. And a low score is not always a memory failure: the authors traced the 32K Transformer's 0.35 on variable tracking to copying the worked example's answer.

Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

blocks.question: A team must cut KV memory but keeps exact recall at 200K tokens. Which design is riskiest?
options: 1 full attention layer per 8 layers, Mamba-2 elsewhere
Mamba layers plus only 2048-token sliding window attention
Gated DeltaNet with a full attention layer every 4 layers
Parallel attention and SSM heads with global attention in the first, middle and last layers
blocks.explain: With only sliding window attention, no layer can look up a token 200K positions back exactly; that recall must survive inside the fixed Mamba state. The other three keep at least a few global attention layers that can read the whole KV cache.

blocks.question: In the Mamba-2 ablation, why is 24 of 48 attention layers worse than 6, beyond just costing more memory?
options: Attention layers cannot be trained with Mamba-2 layers
Too many attention layers cause the SSM state to overflow
Perplexity itself got worse (8.50 vs 8.26) at the same parameter count, so the extra attention displaced more useful SSM layers
The model ran out of position embeddings
blocks.explain: At fixed parameters, every attention layer replaces an SSM layer. The paper measured quality peaking near 10% attention, so going to 50% both raised perplexity and multiplied the KV cache by 4 compared with 6 layers.

blocks.question: Your hybrid is fine on single-document QA but drops on multi-document QA built by packing unrelated passages. What is the most plausible cause based on the NVIDIA study?
options: The attention layers lack RoPE
The SSM layers' state gets confused by irrelevant documents, possibly from training on packed unrelated sequences
The KV cache is too large
The MLP ratio is too high
blocks.explain: Waleffe et al. hypothesized that SSM states are confused by documents irrelevant to the question, and that their long-context recipe of packing unrelated sequences may teach the SSM layers to treat separate documents as related.

lessons.title: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer

blocks.md:
So far the recipe has had one shape: many SSM or linear layers with a few full attention layers interleaved. Published models vary it along four axes:

1. **What attention sees**: the whole context (global) or only a recent window (sliding-window, or local, attention).
2. **How the mixers combine**: in separate layers (sequential), side by side inside a layer (parallel heads), or one attention block whose weights are reused at several depths (shared).
3. **Which recurrent mixer**: a vector recurrence, Mamba-2, plain linear attention, or delta-rule layers such as Gated DeltaNet and KDA.
4. **How you get the model**: pretrain from scratch, or convert a pretrained Transformer.

Below is one model per axis, read from its paper or config.

**Local attention plus a vector recurrence: Griffin.** Griffin (De et al., Google DeepMind, 2024) uses the RG-LRU (real-gated linear recurrent unit), whose state is one number per channel, a vector rather than a matrix: $h_t = a_t \odot h_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-a_t^2} \odot (i_t \odot x_t)$. Here $\odot$ multiplies entry by entry, $i_t$ is a sigmoid input gate, and $a_t = a^{c\,r_t}$ raises a learned per-channel decay $a$ in (0, 1) to a power set by a sigmoid recurrence gate $r_t$ and the constant $c = 8$. The layers repeat a pattern of two recurrent blocks then one local multi-query attention block (all query heads share one key head and one value head), with a 1,024-token window in Griffin and 2,048 in [RecurrentGemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07839). No layer attends globally, so memory stays constant at any length.

The cost is that exact recall beyond the window must survive in a small vector state. Griffin's authors tested a phone-book lookup on their pretrained 7B Hawk (RG-LRU only), 7B Griffin and 6B Transformer. Griffin solved it perfectly while the phone book fit in its 1,024-token window and degraded once it did not; Hawk failed as the phone book grew; the Transformer was near perfect up to its training length and failed beyond it.

**Shared attention: Zamba.** Zyphra's Zamba (7B, about 1T training tokens) is a Mamba backbone with one shared attention block (attention plus MLP) applied after every 6 Mamba blocks. Every call uses the same weights; its input is the current residual stream concatenated with the original token embeddings, and each call has its own output projection. Zamba2 moves to a Mamba-2 backbone, alternates two shared blocks in its larger models, and adds per-call LoRA adapters (small low-rank weight corrections) so each call can specialize. Sharing saves parameters, not cache: each call sees different activations and keeps its own keys and values. The Zamba2 report says the model stores a KV cache for each invocation of the shared blocks, which at its 1:6 ratio is a 6x reduction compared with a Transformer.

**Parallel heads: Falcon-H1.** TII's Falcon-H1 runs attention and Mamba-2 side by side in every layer: both read the same normalized input, their output channels are concatenated before the block's output projection, and an MLP follows. The paper compared fully parallel, this semi-parallel arrangement and fully sequential blocks, and the semi-parallel one did best. The free knob is how many channels each part gets: more attention channels clearly raised the loss, so the models use roughly 2 : 1 : 5 channels for SSM : attention : MLP. Hymba, from the ratio lesson, is another parallel design.

The cache consequence is the opposite of interleaving: every layer has attention, with few heads. Falcon-H1-7B has 44 layers with 2 KV heads of dimension 128 each ([config](https://huggingface.co/tiiuae/Falcon-H1-7B-Base/blob/main/config.json)), so $2 \times 44 \times 2 \times 128 \times 2$ bytes = 44 KiB per token, against 16 KiB for Nemotron-H-8B.

blocks.title: Layer layouts, first layers of each model

scenes.caption: Griffin: two RG-LRU blocks (R), then one local attention block (L), repeated. No global attention anywhere, so the KV cache is capped at the window.
Zamba: Mamba blocks (M) with a shared attention block (S) after every 6. Every S has the same weights, but each call keeps its own KV.
Falcon-H1: every layer runs attention and Mamba-2 in parallel (A+M). Attention, and so KV, in all 44 layers, but only 2 KV heads each.
MiniMax-Text-01: 7 lightning attention layers (Lin, a linear attention) then 1 softmax attention layer (A), 80 layers in all.
Kimi Linear: 3 KDA layers (K) then 1 MLA layer (A). The released 48B config has 27 layers, 7 of them MLA, the last one at the very end.

blocks.md:
**Linear-attention hybrids at scale.** MiniMax-Text-01 (2025) has 456B parameters with 45.9B active per token and places one softmax attention layer after every 7 lightning attention layers, 80 layers in all. Lightning attention is the additive linear attention from the previous course, computed block by block. The authors chose the hybrid after finding that pure lightning attention had limited retrieval ability. Its successor MiniMax-M2 went back to full attention, citing multi-hop reasoning deficits at scale and hard prefix caching and speculative decoding ([blog](https://www.minimax.io/news/why-did-m2-end-up-as-a-full-attention-model)).

Kimi Linear (Moonshot AI, 2025) mixes Kimi Delta Attention (KDA, from the previous course) with multi-head latent attention (MLA, which caches one compressed vector per token) at a uniform 3:1 ratio, and uses no position encoding in the MLA layers, leaving position to KDA. Trained with the same 1.4T-token recipe as a full-MLA model, it beat it while cutting KV cache by up to 75% and reaching up to 6x decoding throughput at 1M tokens of context.

blocks.title: Kimi Linear ratio ablation: validation perplexity above the best

scenes.caption: Validation perplexity by KDA : MLA ratio: 5.77, 5.66, 5.65, 5.70 and 5.82 (Kimi Linear, Table 1). Pure full attention is worse than every hybrid except 15:1.
1:1 is nearly as good as 3:1 but keeps twice the KV-cache layers; 7:1 matched 3:1 on training loss but was worse on validation. Same flat-then-rising shape as the Mamba-2 ablation.

blocks.md: **Converting instead of pretraining.** Pretraining a hybrid costs trillions of tokens. Mamba in the Llama (Wang, Paliotta et al., 2024) turns a trained Transformer into one. Attention and a Mamba layer have matching pieces: the attention's query, key and value projections initialize Mamba's C, B and x projections, and only the decay A and step size $\Delta$ are new, so a converted layer starts out roughly as linear attention with the teacher's weights. The MLPs are kept and frozen in the first stage. Attention layers are replaced stepwise (keep every second one, distill, then keep every fourth) and training has three stages: distillation on answers generated by the teacher, supervised fine-tuning, then direct preference optimization (DPO: training on pairs of preferred and rejected answers). The whole process uses about 20B tokens; a 50% attention model took under five days on eight 80 GB A100 GPUs. The 50% hybrids matched their teachers on chat benchmarks; the 25% and 12.5% ones were slightly worse.

LoLCATs (Zhang et al.) pushes the budget lower. Step one, **attention transfer**: replace each softmax attention with a linear attention plus a 64-token sliding window of softmax attention inside the same layer, and train only the new feature maps to reproduce the original layer's outputs under a mean squared error loss. Step two: recover quality with LoRA. It uses 40M tokens, and the authors linearized Llama 3.1 70B and 405B. Note the design difference: LoLCATs keeps no global attention layer at all, so exact recall beyond 64 tokens rests on the linear state.

Worked example. A Llama-3-8B-style model has 32 layers with 8 KV heads of dimension 128: 128 KiB of KV per token. Convert it keeping 1 attention layer in 4: 8 attention layers, 32 KiB per token, a 4x smaller KV cache at long context, plus a fixed Mamba state that sets a crossover length as in the cache lesson. At 131,072 tokens that is 16 GiB down to 4 GiB per sequence. The training budget is about 20B tokens for the Mamba in the Llama recipe, against the roughly 15T tokens Llama 3 was pretrained on, about 0.13%.

A converted hybrid starts from its teacher, but the attention fraction is still a quality dial: the distilled models with 25% and 12.5% attention scored below the 50% ones. Measure recall on the converted model (an MQAR-style probe or RULER) rather than assuming the teacher's.

Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

blocks.question: A team needs exact recall of a fact stated 50,000 tokens earlier. Which design can look it up exactly rather than relying on a compressed state?
options: Griffin-style: recurrent blocks plus 2,048-token local attention
LoLCATs-style: linear attention plus a 64-token window in every layer
Zamba-style: Mamba blocks plus a shared global attention block
Pure Mamba-2 with a larger state
blocks.explain: Only the shared block attends globally: its KV cache holds all 50,000 tokens for each call. The two windowed designs can see exact tokens only within their windows, and any pure recurrent state compresses.

blocks.question: Zamba-7B applies one shared attention block at 13 depths. Compared with 13 separate attention layers of the same shape, its KV cache is:
options: 13x smaller, since the weights are shared
Zero, since shared layers need no cache
Half as large
The same size, since each call sees different activations
blocks.explain: Weights are shared, activations are not: each call computes its own keys and values from a different residual stream, so each needs its own cache. The Zamba paper states this directly (independent KV-cache entries at each invocation), and so does Zamba2's report; the saving is in parameters.

blocks.question: You convert a 32-layer Transformer with 128 KiB of KV per token into a hybrid that keeps 1 attention layer in 8. How much KV per token remains?
options: 16 KiB
32 KiB
4 KiB
64 KiB
blocks.explain: KV is per attention layer: 128 KiB / 32 layers = 4 KiB per layer, and 4 layers remain, so 16 KiB, an 8x saving at long context. The Mamba layers add a fixed state that does not grow with context.
